en: Sūtra: For what reason? The Commentary states: From here on, it is explained specifically. There are two parts: first, the inquiry;
second, the explanation. This is the inquiry. For what reason are the lands of sentient beings the lands that are to be adorned?
Sūtra: "All good sons [proceed] to the most adorned and pure Buddha-lands. Commentary: Below there are five layers;
the old version had four, lacking this second one.

It is also possible to combine the two new [categories] into one old [category], naming it "taking up a Buddha-land in accordance with the transformation of sentient beings. Although the principle is likewise the same, its meaning is difficult to comprehend.
The fivefold division is twofold:
the first two stages clarify that, in accordance with sentient beings' arousal of the mind and their practice, one gathers those beings to adorn the Buddha-land;

the latter three stages clarify that, in accordance with how sentient beings should be brought to maturity by means of such an adorned and purified Buddha-land, one accordingly accepts such a Buddha-land.
Alternatively, in the first case, one gathers those born as ordinary worldlings (*bālapṛthagjana*) to adorn the *nirmāṇakāya* land;
in the latter case, one gathers those born prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) to adorn the *saṃbhogakāya* land.
Alternatively, in the first case, one gathers beings; in the latter, one gathers practices.
Although these two meanings differ, adorning the lands of sentient beings is itself the adornment of the Buddha-land.
Within the first [section], there are two parts:
the first reiterates the generation of goodness and the departure from evil among sentient beings, which is precisely the inclusion of adornment and purification.
Later, it further clarifies that when sentient beings initiate merit and wisdom, this already includes the adornment and purification;
or, it may clarify at the outset that when sentient beings resolve their minds and practice, this already includes the adornment and purification;
and later clarify that when sentient beings give rise to other merits, this also includes the adornment and purification.
Alternatively, the initial clarification that sentient beings obtain happiness and leave suffering already encompasses the adornment and purification;
the subsequent clarification that sentient beings increase goodness and extinguish evil likewise encompasses the adornment and purification.
There are three successive layers of meaning, and this is the first passage.
It is for the sake of increase because it gives rise to the wholesome, or because it generates the resolve [for awakening], or because it attains happiness.
It is for the sake of benefit because it brings about freedom from evil, or because it constitutes spiritual practice, or because it brings about freedom from suffering.

The old translation states: "One takes up a buddha-field according to the sentient beings to be converted. This is consistent with the first two layers [of meaning]; it is also acceptable to refer to the sentient beings who are benefited as "beings to be converted."
Sūtra: Following all sentient beings to the adorned and pure Buddha-lands. Commentary:
This second section clarifies the arousal of merit and wisdom in accordance with sentient beings.
Arising other merits, increasing the wholesome and diminishing the unwholesome, one thereby gathers those beings to adorn the Buddha-field.
For each of these, there are three successive explanations.
Sūtra: "According to the various sentient beings, they arrive at such a Buddha-field."
The commentary states:

Below are three layers that clarify how, in accordance with sentient beings who should be matured by means of such adorned and purified Buddha-lands, one accordingly takes possession of such Buddha-lands.
Within this, there are two parts:
the first part concerns how sentient beings, by means of such a purified Buddha-field as they require, attain the cessation of evil, thereby encompassing that field;
the latter two parts clarify how sentient beings, by means of such a purified Buddha-field as they require, are able to acquire goodness, thereby encompassing that field.
This is the first passage.
"To subdue" means to harmonize and control the activities of body and speech, thereby restraining and eliminating all afflictions and karma.

Regarding the phrase "one should adorn and purify such a Buddha-field": practicing all the supreme deeds of a bodhisattva is called "adorned and purified land. Because it is the cause for adorning and purifying the land, the cultivation of that cause is termed "adorning."

The meaning here is as follows: according to the needs of sentient beings, whatever sublime practices of a bodhisattva can cause them to cease evil, those very practices are then embraced—just as one maintains precepts oneself and subdues the evils of others—for the purpose of purifying buddha-fields is fundamentally for the sake of benefiting living beings.
Sūtra: "He goes to such Buddha-lands wherever sentient beings may be. Commentary:
These two sections clarify that by following sentient beings and thereby attaining virtue, he encompasses these lands.
There are two parts:
first, it clarifies the goodness of attaining the fruit for those who have not yet attained it; second, it clarifies the goodness of attaining the cause for those who have not yet attained it.
"Buddha-wisdom" refers to the goodness of the fruit.
The practitioner of the noble faculties (*āryendriya*) does so by virtue of the wholesome.
That which attains the noble faculties is the bodhicitta; that which follows thereafter is the noble practice (*āryacaryā*).
Alternatively, the noble faculties refer to the five beginning with faith (*śraddhā*), while the noble practices refer to the remaining myriad deeds.
Alternatively, "the noble one" refers to the Buddha; "noble faculties" (āryendriya) are the practice, for it is by taking practice as the foundation that one attains nobility.
Alternatively, "noble faculties" are untainted wisdom (anāsravaprajñā), while "noble practice" refers to the other causes [for that attainment].
Sūtra: "For what reason? [It is] because of the merit of ultimate purity. Commentary:
This is the third explanation of the underlying cause.
The text consists of two parts:
first, the explanation of the underlying cause; second, the illustration by means of an analogy.
This is the first part, which begins with a question followed by an answer.
The intent of the question here is this: it was previously stated that the very lands of sentient beings constitute the bodhisattva’s purified buddha-field; what is the reason for this?
Now, however, it is said that by providing superior benefit to sentient beings, one gathers them in and thereby adorns that field.

The Buddha said, "Good son, the root of a bodhisattva consists in embracing and purifying buddha-fields. Whatever they do is performed solely for the sake of increasing the benefit and welfare of sentient beings and for giving rise to pure merit; it is not for anything else. Therefore, the increase of the benefit and welfare of sentient beings and so forth constitute their buddha-fields."

If sentient beings do not increase wholesome dharmas, provide benefit and happiness, or give rise to pure merit, they are not those transformed by the Buddha, nor are they part of the Bodhisattva’s purified buddha-field.
The meaning of the old text is summarized here, though there are slight differences.
The Sūtra says: "O sons of good family... until finally they cannot achieve it.
The commentary states:
The following uses analogies to clarify this.
First the analogy, then the application; this is the analogy.
This analogy consists of four parts:
First, the great earth; second, the open space; third, the adornment of the palaces; and fourth, the void.
As for that adornment, it is adorned with all kinds of rare jewels.
Just as people do not establish palaces upon empty ground, for they cannot be completed there—
so too does a bodhisattva proceed in this manner to such-and-such a buddha-field. Commentary:
This is the lower correspondence.
The person is like the bodhisattva, and empty space is like that which is grasped.
Since the essence of the person-dharma is non-existent, and because dharmas are fundamental, one speaks only of the emptiness of dharmas.
That empty space is a metaphor for the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature).

The fact that all sentient beings construct palaces, chambers, and ornaments therein is a metaphor for those sentient beings increasing their benefits and generating pure merit; by realizing the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature), they then take possession of such a buddha-field.
Sūtra: “...upholding [the land] in this manner, up to: it is not by means of emptiness. Commentary:

With the exception of Bodhisattvas, all other sentient beings cannot possibly succeed in purifying a Buddha-field by means of the empty and non-existent phenomena they grasp. This, conversely, reveals that one must necessarily increase the pure merit that benefits and enriches sentient beings—who exist as dependent nature—in order to realize the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Sūtra: Furthermore, from the passage "The nature of the jewel" up to "will be born in that land.
Commentary: This concludes the second response concerning the causes for the adornment and purification [of the Buddha-field].
Within this, there are two parts:

first, the answer regarding the causes of adornment; second, from the passage "Good sons, when a bodhisattva thus gives rise to the bodhicitta" onwards, the revelation of the benefits for which the causes of the land are intended.
Now there are eighteen practices for purifying the Buddha-land; previously there were seventeen, lacking this third one.
Within these eighteen sections, they are divided into seven:
the first four are as stated in the text, while the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā) are combined and named "the cessation of all hindrances."
The four immeasurables, the four means of attraction, skillful means, and the factors of enlightenment—these four dharmas are called the teaching on "arousing.
The three consisting of ceasing the unfavorable states, maintaining one's own ethical conduct, and the ten paths of wholesome action are called "quiescence."
Each contains two parts:
the first all set forth the causal practice, and the latter all reveal the attainment of the fruit.
This is the initial translation.
If bodhisattvas give rise to the mind of unsurpassed awakening, this is precisely the cause for adorning and purifying their future buddha-fields.

Since the preceding passage stated that the realm of sentient beings constitutes the bodhisattva’s field for adorning and purifying the buddha-field, it follows that the very place where the bodhisattva gives rise to their own mind is itself the cause of adornment.
Since the internal causes are thus, external conditions give rise to sentient beings of the Mahāyāna who have not yet been born in that land.
In the older translation, this corresponds to the third [stage], the Great Bodhicitta.
It takes the five faculties as its essence and great vows as its condition, employing non-retrogression as the means of incitement.
All other meanings are as explained in the *Youzan* (Profound Commentary).
Question:
The *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states, "The perfection of the causes for the Pure Land arises from supramundane roots of goodness that are superior."
Why does this assembly state that the arousal of the thought of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*) and so forth are the causes for the Pure Land? Answer:
They rely upon the primary cause (*hetu*), which is capable of reversing [delusion] and capable of guiding practice; its nature is solely wisdom (*jñāna*).

This is based on the essential point that the fulfillment of the myriad practices alone brings about the realization of a pure land; therefore, it is not contradictory for the arousal of the bodhicitta and other such factors to be considered causes for a pure land.
As the *Sūtra on the Land of Pure Intention* states: "Until one is born in that land."
The commentary states:
This is the second section.
In Sanskrit it is called *adhyāśaya*, which is translated as "intention" (*yìlè*).
Being unmixed with evil is called "pure intention" (*āśaya*), because the intention is pure within.
Because they cultivate inner purity, uprightness, and rectitude, sentient beings who are free from flattery, crookedness, and deceitful flaws will come to be born in that land.

The old [translation] says "direct mind" (*ṛju-citta*). Although the essence of the direct mind is purely intentional (*āśaya*), it is so called because there is no crookedness due to delusion (*moha*).
Sūtra: From the Land of Skillful Application (*sukṛta-prayoga*) until arriving in that country.
The commentary states:
This has not existed previously.
To skillfully cultivate merit and wisdom according to one's efforts is called "wholesome preparatory application" (*sābhisaṃskāra*).
Therefore, there are sentient beings who give rise to virtuous conduct and those who maintain and do not abandon virtuous conduct who come to be born [therein].
The essence of preparatory application (*prayoga*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), or these may also pertain to all virtues.
Sūtra: “With a superior intention, one will go to that land and be reborn in that realm.
Commentary: “Superior” (*adhimātra*) means preeminent (*udbhūta*).

Whenever one practices virtue, the arousal of a superior, intense, and powerful impulse is called "superior intention" (*adhyāśaya*); therefore, through such virtuous dharmas, sentient beings are brought into birth.
The older translation, "the superior and intense intention of the profound mind," is also correct because it refers to the profound mind; however, the meaning is somewhat obscured by the phrasing.
Sūtra: By practicing the perfection of giving, one will be reborn in that land in a future life.
Commentary: Herein, the six perfections are collectively termed "quiescence" (*śamatha*), because they quiesce all obstacles.
Its essential nature is as previously described.

Generosity eliminates stinginess and externally brings about the capacity for relinquishment; ethical discipline abandons the defilement of transgression. Since these constitute the ten paths of wholesome action, they bring about the rebirth of sentient beings who practice those ten virtues.
Through patience (*kṣānti*), one eliminates anger; thus, one is able to bring forth the thirty-two marks (*dvātriṃśan mahāpuruṣalakṣaṇa*) to adorn one's own body.
These thirty-two marks shall be explained in detail below.
By enduring the injuries of others, one externally brings about the capacity to endure all forms of suffering.
Through the patience of acceptance (*adhivāsanā-kṣānti*), one externally brings about gentleness;
through the patience of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇā-kṣānti*), one externally brings about the rebirth of peaceful sentient beings.
Previous accounts merely state that "beings with the thirty-two marks come to be born," which is logically inconsistent with this [explanation].
Diligence eliminates indolence, and its external effects can be known.
Concentration eliminates distraction; therefore, one who possesses mindfulness knows that they will be reborn in a state of concentration.

Because concentration is attained through right mindfulness, and because concentration arises from hearing and reflection—since the essence of the two types of wisdom, hearing and reflection, consists of correct knowledge.
Furthermore, through mindfulness one attains concentration, and through concentration wisdom arises; for wisdom is precisely right knowledge (*saṃprajanya*).
This phrase "right mindfulness and right knowledge" is absent from the older edition.
Because wisdom eliminates ignorance, it brings about the birth of sentient beings who have entered the state of a noble one (*ārya*).
Those who enter right concentration attain the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) and so forth.
This collection consists of three parts:
1. The group of those fixed in the right [path] (*samyaktva-niyata-rāśi*), because they have entered the path of vision (*darśana-mārga*).
2. The group of those fixed in the wrong [path] (*mithyātva-niyata-rāśi*), namely those with various false views.
3. The group of those not fixed [in either] (*aniyata-rāśi*), because they are the remainder after excluding the other two.
Entering right concentration (*samyaksamādhi*) refers to the right concentration of the noble ones (*ārya*), though it also extends to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
Concentration born of faith (*śraddhāsamādhi*) is likewise called right concentration, as it does not contradict the principle.
Sūtra: "The four immeasurables (*apramāṇa*) lead to rebirth in that land."
The commentary states:
Below are four sections concerning the "Initiation of Renown," because once obstacles have been removed, one initiates what is wholesome.
This is analyzed by means of five gates:

First, the enumeration of names; second, the explanation of names; third, the analysis of their modes of activity; fourth, the determination of their essential natures; fifth, the analysis of their distinctions. Regarding the enumeration of names:
they are loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).

Regarding the explanation of the names, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 12, states: "Because these four arise by taking immeasurable objects as their conditions and universally taking all sentient beings as their objects."
It is called "immeasurable" because it gives rise to immeasurable practices, and because the practice and understanding are likewise utterly vast;
it brings about immeasurable fruits, attains the merit of Great Brahmā, and achieves the state of a Tathāgata.
"Fourth is the number; this is an explanation by means of a numeral.
To distinguish the characteristics of the practice: sentient beings within the dharma-realm are generally categorized into three classes:
first, those who experience neither suffering nor pleasure. Bestowing happiness upon them without inversion is called *maitrī* (loving-kindness), which has non-hatred as its essence."
Second, regarding those who possess suffering, to extract their suffering is called compassion (*karuṇā*);
its essence is non-harming. Third, regarding those who possess happiness, to assist in their joy is sympathetic joy (*muditā*); its nature is the root of goodness that is free from envy.

Furthermore, toward those who possess neither suffering nor happiness, one gives rise to the thought of being free from delusion; toward those who possess suffering, one gives rise to the thought of being free from hatred; and toward those who possess happiness, one gives rise to the thought of being free from attachment. Because one desires with equanimity that they be freed from all evils, it is called equanimity (*upekṣā*); because it causes the relinquishing of evil, its essence is wholesome relinquishment.
Regarding their essential nature: they now take three dharmas as their essence, namely, non-aversion (*adveṣa*), non-harming (*ahiṃsā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Regarding their distinctions: each of these has three types;
first, those with sentient beings as their object, wherein one forms the perception of a sentient being.
The second is the object-conditioned [compassion], which does not perceive sentient beings but forms a conceptualization of dharmas alone.
Subsequently, regarding all dharmas, one abandons the mind of discrimination and forms a conceptualization of *tathatā* (suchness); this is called the "objectless" [compassion].
Among these three, the first is shared with non-Buddhists, the second is shared with those of the Two Vehicles, and the last belongs exclusively to Bodhisattvas.
The first two bring about peace and happiness, while the last brings about benefit; the resulting fruits may thus be known.
Sūtra: [The section on] the Four Means of Attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) and the Land where one is reborn in that realm.
Commentary: This is analyzed through three gates: first, the explanation of the names; second, the discernment of their characteristics; and third, the determination of their essence.
Regarding the explanation of the names: these four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) gather in sentient beings, causing them to turn toward Bodhi and attain supreme fruits;

therefore, they are called "means of attraction. Regarding the discernment of their characteristics: first is generosity (*dāna*). As for its distinction from the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*), the latter bestows material wealth upon others, whereas this [means of attraction] subsequently gathers them in; thus, there is a difference between the two.

Second is pleasant speech: constantly speaking words that are agreeable, truthful, in accordance with the Dharma, and conducive to the goal; remaining free from harshness and sarcasm; speaking first with a smile; greeting others, inviting them to sit, and inquiring after their well-being; providing appropriate consolation and encouragement; and so forth, as extensively explained—relying upon the four types of pure speech to give rise to the eight noble forms of speech and the three types of beneficial conduct.

By means of pleasant speech, he first demonstrates the correct principle and, according to the precepts studied, exhorts, disciplines, establishes, and settles others with a compassionate and untainted mind. He causes them to obtain wealth and status, to leave the household life and abandon desire, and to attain pliancy and liberation; as it is explained at length, even when undergoing great suffering, they feel redoubled joy, and though dwelling in wealth and status, they remain humble and self-effacing, like slaves, servants, *mīṭhala*, or filial sons.

Regarding the four matters of consolidation: by means of these benefits, if one encourages others to train while also training oneself, it causes the roots of goodness of others to become firm and non-retrogressive; because they have seen what has been practiced, they increase their cultivation twofold. Since this originally gathers sentient beings and directs them toward Bodhi, when the fruit is attained, liberated sentient beings come to be born in that land.

Regarding their essential nature: generosity has non-attachment and the three types of action as its nature; affectionate speech has verbal action as its nature; beneficial conduct and cooperation have all three types of action as their nature.
These two factors together constitute its nature, namely non-attachment and volition (*cetanā*).
[The Sūtra says: "Through skillful means, they reach the land and are born in that realm. Commentary:
Skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) is the function of wisdom.
This is of two kinds:
first, dedication (*pariṇāmanā*); second, deliverance (*uddharaṇa*). Together there are twelve types, which shall be explained below.

Because of these two skillful means—dedication (*pariṇāmana*) and deliverance (*uddharaṇa*)—when the fruit is attained, one skillfully contemplates all phenomena and the arising of sentient beings; this is due to the skillfulness of the cause of wisdom.

The *Old Sūtra* states, "Skillful means regarding all phenomena are unimpeded," which also carries the sense of skillful contemplation, having the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) as its essence.
Sūtra: By practicing the thirty-seven [factors], one will be reborn in that land in a future life.

Commentary: These thirty-seven factors shall be briefly analyzed by way of five sections: first, the explanation of the general name; second, the clarification of their numerical categories; third, the identification of their essential nature (*svabhāva*); fourth, the elucidation of the stages of cultivation; and fifth, the distinction between those with outflows (*sāsrava*) and those without outflows (*anāsrava*).
To explain the general meaning of the name: *bodhi* has the sense of "awakening," which refers to the fruit of Buddhahood sought;
*aṅga* has the sense of "factor" or "cause. These thirty-seven [factors] serve as the causes for the fruit of awakening, and are thus called the *bodhipakṣyadharma* (Factors of Awakening).
Second, the explanation of the stages and their enumeration, which briefly comprises seven stages:
first, the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*); because mindfulness clearly records and wisdom dwells upon the object, it is named after that which is proximate [to the mind].
There are four kinds:
body, sensation, mind, and phenomena.
The wisdom that contemplates these four is the essence of the foundations of mindfulness.
2. Right Exertion (*samyakprahāṇa*): This consists of four types:
(1) *saṃvara-prahāṇa*, the application of means to abandon unwholesome states that have already arisen;
(2) *prahāṇa-prahāṇa*, the prevention of unwholesome states not yet arisen so that they do not arise.
Third is the abandonment through protection (*anurakṣaṇā-prahāṇa*), which protects already arisen wholesome dharmas so that they increase.
Fourth is the abandonment through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahāṇa*), which cultivates unarisen wholesome dharmas so that they arise.
Because vigor (*vīrya*) functions within these four to effect correct abandonment, they are called the "Right Abandonments" (*samyakprahāṇa*).

Regarding that which can be abandoned, causing what has not yet arisen not to arise and what has already arisen to be eliminated, their essence is diligence; therefore, they are called "Right Exertions" (*samyakprahāṇa*).

Third, the "Bases of Psychic Power" (*ṛddhipāda*): that which possesses wondrous and unimpeded efficacy is called "psychic" (*ṛddhi*), while that upon which the transformative mind relies is called a "base" (*pāda*); their essence is meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
This [basis] is further divided into four, namely: desire, diligence, mind, and investigation.
Because one cultivates meditative concentration for the sake of these four, concentration is called the "basis of spiritual power" (*ṛddhipāda*).
Fourth, the faculties (*indriya*): they are called faculties because they give rise to wholesome dharmas.
5. Powers (*bala*): that which is difficult to subdue or overcome is called a power.
There are five for each of the two [categories], namely faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom; these names constitute their essential nature (*svabhāva*).
Initial cultivation for the sake of the root of goodness is called "roots" (mūla); subsequent cultivation that is difficult to subdue is called "powers" (bala).
Sixth, the factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga): "enlightenment" (bodhi) refers to wisdom (prajñā), and "factors" (aṅga) has the meaning of "parts."
This is of two kinds: first, awakening itself as a factor, which is the awakening-factor of the investigation of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya-saṃbodhyaṅga*);
second, the factors of awakening, which refers to the remaining six, because they are constituent parts of wisdom (*prajñā*).

These are of seven kinds, namely: investigation of dharmas (dharmapravicaya), diligence (vīrya), joy (prīti), mindfulness (smṛti), concentration (samādhi), equanimity (upekṣā), and pliancy (praśrabdhi).
Three of these are universal mental factors with specific objects (viśeṣālambana): investigation of dharmas, mindfulness, and concentration.
Three are wholesome factors (*kuśala-dharma*): diligence (*vīrya*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), and pliancy (*praśrabdhi*).
One is a universal factor (*sarvatraga*), namely the factor of joy (*prīti*).

Seventh are the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*); "path" (*mārga*) refers to the noble path (*āryamārga*), which is the untainted faculty of wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñendriya*), and "factors" (*aṅga*) has the meaning of constituent parts.
First, the path itself is the factor;
second, the factors of the path, which refers to the remaining seven dharmas.
This is as can be understood from what preceded.
In total, there are eight: namely, right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right mindfulness, right concentration, and right effort.
Right thought has wisdom as its nature, because within the Buddha’s body there is no vitarka or vicāra.
Right speech and right action are the bodily and vocal expressions produced by the absence of hatred and delusion.

The bodily and vocal actions produced by the single factor of non-attachment are termed right livelihood (*samyagājīva*); it is established as a separate category in contrast to the five forms of wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*).
These three—right view, right resolve, and right livelihood—have both unmanifest form (*avijñapti-rūpa*) and volition (*cetanā*) as their essential nature.
Regarding the clarification of their essential nature: among the thirty-seven factors, there are nine that constitute the body [of the path]:
first, wisdom; second, diligence; third, concentration; fourth, resolve; fifth, mindfulness; sixth, joy; seventh, equanimity; eighth, pliancy; and ninth, non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*).
Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 57, states: "The five faculties, such as faith and the rest, are not subsumed within the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
Which ones? There are six dharmas: joy (*prīti*), tranquility (*praśrabdhi*), equanimity (*upekṣā*), speech (*vāk*), action (*karma*), and livelihood (*ājīva*)."
The three—vitality (*jīvita*), karma (*karman*), and non-informative matter (*avijñapti*)—are thus [included].
Among these, there is one universal mental factor (*sarvatraga*), namely joy (*saumanasya*).
There are three object-specific factors (*viṣayapratiniyata*), namely mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).
"There are four wholesome [factors]: faith, diligence, equanimity, and pliancy.
There is one material phenomenon, namely, non-informative matter (*avijñapti-rūpa*).
This describes the state of Buddhahood.
If it is not the stage of Buddhahood, ten factors constitute its essence.
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Correct reflection (samyak-saṃkalpa) is untainted vitarka (anāsrava-vitarka).
Regarding this, there are two interpretations; the present meaning is the correct one."

Regarding the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanāvasthā*): the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), and the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*) pertain to this.

The initial cultivation occurs during the stage of the wholesome roots conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*). The five faculties (*pañcendriya*) pertain to the stages of "heat" (*uṣmagata*) and "summit" (*mūrdhan*). The five powers (*pañcabala*) pertain to the stages of "patience" (*kṣānti*) and the "highest mundane dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*). The seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) pertain to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), and the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*) pertains to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Regarding the distinction between the contaminated (*sāsrava*) and the uncontaminated (*anāsrava*), this can only be understood by way of the stages (*avasthā*).

Prior to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), there is only the contaminated; from the path of seeing onward, it may be either contaminated or uncontaminated; and at the stage of Buddhahood, it is exclusively uncontaminated.
The detailed explanation of its characteristics is as described in the *Abhidharma*. The Sūtra states:
"Cultivating the dedication [of merit] to the land until it is adorned with all virtues.
The Commentary says:
This seventh section concerns dedication (*pariṇāmanā*): whatever wholesome roots one cultivates are dedicated toward Bodhi; this is called dedication.
Because one does not seek rebirth in saṃsāra, when the fruit is attained, that land will be fully adorned with all manner of virtues.
Dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) is itself an aspiration; it is an aspiration directed toward enlightenment because it encompasses all objective spheres.
Aspiration has faith, desire, and resolute conviction as its essence.
The Sūtra says: "It is well explained as the pacification [of afflictions] and the attainment of the state free from the lack of leisure."
The commentary states:
Below there are three sections, collectively named "Quiescence," because they quiesce two kinds of evil.
The first is the quiescence of the eight difficulties, which is the quiescence of evil fruits.
The second [point] is the pacification of transgressions against the prohibitions and the ten paths of unwholesome action; this is the pacification of the causes of evil.
This is the first section of the text.

Regarding the eight states of no-leisure (*aṣṭākṣaṇa*), formerly called the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāvaraṇa*): one constantly undergoes manifold sufferings and lacks even a moment’s leisure to cultivate wholesome deeds or seek awakening.

The eight states of non-leisure (*aṣṭāv akṣaṇāḥ*) are as follows: the three evil destinies constitute three; the four types of those with impaired faculties, such as those who are blind from birth, deaf, or mute; the fifth is those who possess worldly wit and eloquence yet hold evil and false views; the sixth is being born before or after a Buddha; the seventh is being born in Uttarakuru; and the eighth is the long-lived heavens, meaning birth among the non-noble gods within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
According to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, the four wheels of gods and humans can destroy the eight difficulties (*aṣṭākṣaṇa*):

first, dwelling in a favorable place and being born in a central land; this eliminates five difficulties, namely, the three evil destinies, the northern continent (Uttarakuru), and the long-lived heavens.
Second, relying on virtuous persons, meaning encountering the era of a Buddha; this eliminates one obstacle, namely being born before or after a Buddha's appearance.
Third, generating right aspirations, meaning possessing a mind of right view; this eliminates one obstacle, namely worldly wisdom and cleverness.
Fourth, one plants roots of goodness; this also excludes one [obstacle]: those who are blind, deaf, mute, and so forth.
Furthermore, one cultivates five practices to eliminate these eight difficulties:
first, receiving and upholding the precepts, which remedies rebirth in the three evil realms.
Second, practicing the gift of Dharma with joy, which removes [the obstacle of] being blind or deaf;
third, possessing correct faith and understanding, which removes [the obstacle of] worldly cleverness and erudition;
fourth, associating with virtuous friends, which removes [the obstacle of] being born before or after a Buddha.
One is born in a central land, excluding birth in the northern continent or among the long-lived gods.

A bodhisattva constantly teaches the first four wheels or the subsequent five practices to eliminate the eight states of lack of leisure; therefore, when the fruit is attained, one is free from the three evil destinies and the eight states of lack of leisure.
"Non-leisure" (akṣaṇa) refers to the state in general; "evil destinies" (durgati) refers to it specifically.
The Sūtra [uses] the name ranging from "maintaining one's own observance of the precepts" to "prohibitions.
The commentary says:
Within the state of tranquility, there are two ways in which the causes of evil are suppressed:
first, the arising of evil from within what has been received as good; second, the commission of evil by one's own nature.
This refers to the former.
He maintained the precepts without deficiency, frequently repenting for his own misdeeds, refraining from censuring the faults of others, and being able to praise the virtues of others.

Consequently, when he attained the fruit [of Buddhahood], even the name of "transgressing prohibitions" did not exist in his land, let alone the sight of those who actually committed such transgressions.
Sūtra: From the Ten Paths of Wholesome Action... until being reborn in that land in a future life. Commentary:
This merely stops one from committing evil by one's own nature.
The ten paths of wholesome action are briefly analyzed by way of three sections:
first, the determination of their essential nature; second, the explanation of their names; and third, the discernment of their fruits.
Regarding the determination of their essential nature: abstaining from killing and so forth constitute the first three, which pertain to the body.
Non-false speech and the other [three] constitute the four [virtuous paths of action] of speech;
non-covetousness and the others constitute the last three of the mental [paths].
All take volition (*cetanā*) as their essence, because the essence of all three types of karma is volition.

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "The first seven courses of action also have volition (*cetanā*) as their essence, because it is not only the latter three whose essence is volition; rather, bodily and vocal actions are manifestations of the volition of the mind."

"The manifest action (vijñapti-karman) is a conventional designation; this perfumed seed of volition (cetanā) is conventionally designated as non-manifest form-action (avijñapti-rūpa-karman), but its substance is actually not form.

The *Vyākhyāyukti* (or *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*) states: "The two forms of body and speech are by nature neither good nor evil; because they manifest what is good or evil, they are conventionally designated as good or evil; therefore, their substance is volition itself."
Volition (*cetanā*) is of three kinds:
first, deliberative volition (*paryeṣaka-cetanā*), because it deliberates upon what is to be done;
second, determinative volition (*niścita-cetanā*), because it determines that one will act.
"Because it is the third [factor], the movement that initiates volition, which actually gives rise to action;
therefore, this third factor is taken as the essence of the path of action (*karmapatha*).

Second, regarding the explanation of the names: 'ten' (*daśa*) refers to the number. 'Wholesome' (*kuśala*) has the meaning of conforming to principle and benefiting sentient beings. 'Action' (*karman*) has the meaning of performing or creating. 'Path' (*patha*) has the meaning of that which is traversed and the meaning of being able to lead to rebirth."

These categories of volition (*cetanā*) are named ten; that which is capable of producing benefit is called "wholesome" (*kuśala*), and that whose essence is capable of performing action is called "karma.

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "This third [type of] volition is called a 'path' (*mārga*) because it is traversed by the former two types of volition and because it universally produces future results of maturation (*vipākaphala*) and so forth."
Regarding "wandering and treading," the meaning of being induced by discursive thought is the same as in the *Karmasiddhiprakaraṇa*.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 60, states: "Volition (*cetanā*) is karma, but it is not a path of action (*karmapatha*)."
From killing up to frivolous speech, these are both karma and paths of action (*karmapatha*).

Regarding covetousness, malice, and wrong view, they are paths of action but not karma; this is because it follows the principle of "concomitant turning" (*anuvartana*) and accords with the explanations of the Sarvāstivādins and others.
According to the gateway of ultimate truth in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, that [third thought] is likewise a gateway of ultimate truth; the intention of that treatise states:

if a course of action (*karmapatha*) can be called a "path" (*mārga*) because it is traversed by the volition (*cetanā*) that performs the act, then the third volition is not given the name "path" because it is not traversed by the volition that constitutes the course of action.

In the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, it is stated that only the third type of volition (cetanā)—that which is "traversed by others" and "universally productive of future results"—is designated by the name of a "path of action" (*karmapatha*);
thus, there is no contradiction.

Furthermore, because the informative acts of body and speech are issued by volition (*cetanā*), they are metaphorically designated as "karma" (action). Because they are what is performed and that which is traversed by volition, they are metaphorically termed "paths of karma" (*karmapatha*).

Based on this, the *Yogācārabhūmi* further states: "From killing up to frivolous speech, these are both karma and paths; yet in reality they are not karma, but can be called paths, because they are not the actual agents."
"The three [factors] beginning with wrong view are no different from one another.
To explain these specific names, they may be understood by reversing the term "evil" (*akuśala*), as found in the eighth and ninth fascicles of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.

Third, regarding the analysis of the fruits: wholesome contaminated (*sāsrava*) paths of action obtain four fruits, excluding the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*); uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) wholesome paths of action obtain four fruits, excluding the fruit of maturation (*vipāka-phala*). If these mutually support one another, each obtains five fruits. One should understand this by applying the same logic as when each of the ten unwholesome paths of action was explained in reverse.
Regarding what is here called the "extremely pure ten paths of wholesome action": the untainted (anāsrava) paths of action are termed "extremely pure" because they are not tainted (sāsrava).

It clarifies that at the time of attaining Buddhahood there is no ripened fruit (vipākaphala); rather, by practicing non-killing, one obtains a determined lifespan when the subsequent fruit is realized, and by abstaining from taking what is not given, one becomes greatly wealthy—both of these latter cases being results of outflow (niṣyandaphala).

Because he abstains from sexual misconduct, his conduct is that of a brahmacārin; because he abstains from false speech, his words are truthful; because he abstains from harsh speech, he always uses gentle words. These three [virtues] are all results of dominance (*adhipatiphala*).
Because one has abandoned divisive speech, one’s retinue does not become estranged; this is the flow-on result (*niṣyanda-phala*).
Because one has abandoned frivolous speech, one skillfully proclaims the intended meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*); this is likewise the dominant result (*adhipati-phala*).
By abandoning greed, hatred, and wrong view, one attains the other three [abstinences]; these three are all outflow fruits (*niṣyanda-phala*).

Here, it is stated collectively that the six karmas—abstaining from killing, stealing, divisive speech, greed, hatred, and wrong view—attain outflow fruits, while the remaining four attain dominant fruits (*adhipati-phala*).
Now, by cross-referencing these points, they may be understood according to reason.

Fearing prolixity, I have omitted further elaboration; all details are as extensively explained in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (chapters 8, 9, 59, and 60), the *Abhidharma-samuccaya* (chapter 7), the *Karmasiddhi-prakaraṇa*, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, and so forth.
The old sūtra says, "skillfully reconciling disputes," which is the fruit of not engaging in frivolous speech (*sambhinna-pralāpa*).
Regarding the phrase "because of skillfully proclaiming the implicit meaning" (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*): "implicit meaning" refers to the underlying principle hidden within the words.
If one embellishes words and phrases with flowery rhetoric, it will obscure the underlying principle.
One who speaks with straightforwardness can proclaim the meaning; such speech is invariably beneficial, and this is the fruit of non-greed.
If greed arises, it is because it does not bring benefit.
Envy and anger do not both produce the fruit of hatred,
for the essence of envy is itself hatred.
If one relies on the new text, there will be no further doubt or difficulty.
The Sūtra says: "O sons of good family, when one arrives, there is tranquility.
The commentary states:
From here below is the second section, which reveals the causes for adorning the land and the benefits intended therefrom.
This section contains seventeen turns in total, which are divided into two parts:
the first eight turns enumerate the sequential order of the eighteen types of practices mentioned above, showing how they successively give rise to one another;
The subsequent nine turns of exposition clarify the superior fruits produced by the causes for adorning the buddha-field;
this is the first section of that text.
Previously there were thirteen turns: the first seven turns recapitulate the various preceding sections, while the final six turns concern the adornment of the field and the fruits produced therein.
Among these, the fifth turning, "Cessation," summarizes the preceding six perfections, as it brings to rest the six obscurations.

This sixth turning, "Initiation," summarizes the preceding four—immeasurables, means of attraction, skillful means, and factors conducive to enlightenment—as they initiate the two types of supreme benefit for oneself and others.

Regarding this eighth "tranquility," it combines the two preceding points: the cessation of the eight [unwholesome states] and the untimely conditions (*akṣaṇa*), while maintaining self-restraint through the precepts and practicing the ten paths of wholesome action, thereby pacifying all evils.

Among the eighteen [causes], the sixteenth is the absence of leisure and the seventeenth is the observance of one's own moral conduct. By cultivating these two causes, one becomes a person who is not a vessel for evil;
by cultivating the remaining sixteen causes, one becomes a vessel that does not contain an evil person.

In the old translation, "direct mind" (*ṛju-citta*) comes first and "practicing the path" (*pratipatti*) comes next; however, "practicing the path" should correspond to "deep mind" (*adhyāśaya*), and "deep mind" should correspond to the "Mahāyāna mind. Thus, the text has been transposed.
The second is "initiation," which is difficult to understand in its underlying principle.

"Subduing" refers back to the aforementioned six perfections; because they subdue the six obscurations, it is as stated regarding the practitioner’s immeasurable bases of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) and the skillful means of the path-factors (*mārgāṅga*); this is due to these four kinds of practice.

The seventh skillful means consists of explaining the eight difficult circumstances, maintaining one's own observance of the precepts, and the ten paths of wholesome action; these three types of superior skillful means are for the purpose of pacifying evil.
Sūtra: "According to their tranquility, they reach the adorned and pure Buddha-fields. Commentary:
Below are nine verses that reveal the supreme fruits produced by the causes for adorning the Buddha-fields.
Within this, there are two parts:
the first two turns clarify how the preceding causes of adornment elicit the fruit of the pure land;
the subsequent seven turns clarify how the pure land, once established, further gives rise to superior fruits.
This is the first passage.
Because the adornment of prior causes brings about superior sentient beings, it is said that "by this there are pure sentient beings.

To abandon evil and cultivate goodness is precisely what Bodhisattvas fundamentally aspire to; this constitutes the purity of the Tathāgata’s Buddha-field, for the field of sentient beings is the Buddha-field.

Once the internal realm of sentient beings has been purified, the external realm of the vessel-world naturally becomes pure as well; for it is through the purity of the mind that the Buddha-field is purified.
Sūtra: "According to the adornment and purity of the Buddha-field, [it is endowed] with all sublime qualities."
The commentary states:
Below are seven sections, clarifying that the Pure Land is established to further produce superior fruits.
Within these, there are two parts:
The first turning is the fruit of benefiting those who transform others;
the subsequent six turnings are the fruits of benefiting those who are transformed.
This has two meanings:
First is the meaning of turning the wheel of Dharma.
Because they arise sequentially from one another, there exist those sentient beings and lands.
Once these have been adorned and purified, one is then able to transform others; thus, there exists the teaching of the Dharma.
Once the Dharma-teachings have been bestowed, they transform beings to produce sublime merit, causing them to be born among gods and humans because they receive superior blessings.
Next, the three types of sublime wisdom—arising from hearing, reflection, and cultivation—develop in conjunction with outflows (*sāsrava*).
Once wondrous wisdom has arisen, untainted knowledge (anāsrava-jñāna) arises.
Once untainted knowledge has arisen, untainted conduct arises.
Once untainted conduct has arisen, all eight consciousnesses are completely purified.
Once the mind has been purified, one attains the perfection of the fruit, being fully endowed with immeasurable and wondrous virtues.
This is further termed the "adornment and purification of the Buddha-field.
Second is the sense of that which can be bestowed upon others.
Once that sentient-being realm has been thus adorned and purified, one may then instruct and transform them by means of the teachings of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
This is because the purification of the sentient-being realm is itself the ten stages.
Once the Dharma-teachings have been bestowed, there arises untainted merit (*anāsrava-puṇya*), because of which one receives various blessings such as the fruits of the ten kings.

Subsequently, non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) arises; once non-conceptual wisdom has arisen, subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*) arises; once subsequently attained wisdom has arisen, untainted practice (*anāsrava-caryā*) arises; once untainted practice has arisen, the eight consciousnesses become pure; once the eight consciousnesses are pure, the myriad virtues are fully perfected, thereby leading to the attainment of Buddhahood.
This vow arises from having already brought forth the fruit of a pure land through the causes of purifying that land; once the fruit of a pure land has been brought forth, this supreme fruit arises.

In the older version of the sutra, there are only four turns here, lacking the two types of "sublime merit" and "sublime practice," and combining wisdom (*jñāna*) and insight (*prajñā*) into a single turn.
Sūtra: From "All good sons" up to "purifying their own minds. Commentary:
Within the extensive discourse of the Tathāgata, this is the second section below, which exhorts the arousal of the mind for purification.
There are two parts:
first, the exhortation; second, the explanation.
This is the former.
Sūtra: "For what reason? [It is] because of attaining a most pure Buddha-field.
Commentary: This explains the reason for [the preceding statement].
When the minds of practitioners are adorned and purified, the external world of sentient beings and their environment likewise becomes pure.
If one’s own mind is not pure, how can one attain a pure land?
Therefore, when the Bodhisattva’s own mind is clear and pure, the sentient beings who are merely provisional constructs of the five aggregates are also pure.
When the internal mind is purified, the external sentient beings and the physical environment are likewise purified.
The *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states: "It is characterized by the most supreme mastery and pure consciousness."
Therefore, when consciousness is pure, the Buddha-field is pure.
Thus far, we have spoken only of sentient beings as the "field," because they are the primary objects of transformation.

We have not yet discussed the receptacle world (bhājanaloka); however, when the field of sentient beings is purified, the receptacle world is naturally purified of its own accord—this was not explicitly stated.
Sūtra: At that time, Śāriputra arrived at such a place of impurity. Commentary:
Within the section on the perfection of causes, there are three parts; from here below is the third, which clarifies and resolves doubts.
Within this, there are four parts:
first, the arising of Śāriputra’s doubt; second, the consolation and encouragement of the Noble One; third, the Buddha’s manifestation of the Pure Land; and fourth, the removal of Śāriputra’s doubt.
This is the first section.
Building upon the previous discussion of purifying the mind, this doubt consequently arises:
"If the mind is pure, the sentient-being world is pure. This refers back to the preceding text regarding the purity of the sentient-being world, the environment, and the purifier.

"Do not say that because my mind was impure, Śākyamuni’s buddha-field is defiled and impure. The word "do not" (mo) here means "must not. The intent of this statement is to clarify: "Is it because my Buddha’s original mind was impure that his buddha-field is now as defiled as this?"

In the language of India, he is called Śāriputra; in the language of Tang, he is called "Spring Warbler. He was named after the mother’s discerning eloquence as a metaphor for her fingers, and because he manifested what she gave birth to, he was called her "son.
Having heard little yet understood much, he was the foremost among the śrāvakas; therefore, the Buddha bestowed his empowerment upon him to give rise to doubts.
Sūtra: The Buddha, knowing his thought, went to him; however, [the man] was blind and could not see.
Commentary: There are two ways in which a noble one comforts and consoles others:
The first parable of the Buddha has three parts:
first, the question; second, the answer; and third, the instruction.
This is the opening passage of the sutra.
The scripture states: "He replied, 'No, it is not the fault of the sun or moon.
The commentary says:
Śāriputra replied. The Sūtra says:
“The Buddha said, ‘It is so... yet you do not see it. Commentary:
The World-Honored One spoke thus.
First, he spoke in general: "Because of the transgressions of sentient beings, they do not see the majestic purity of my buddha-land.
Later, he spoke specifically: "My land is majestic and pure, yet you do not see it."
The *Lotus Sūtra* states: "I always abide here; by means of various supernormal powers, I cause deluded sentient beings not to see me, even though they are near."

Once the sentient beings had gained faith and submission, being upright in character and gentle in mind, they desired with single-minded devotion to see the Buddha, not begrudging their own bodies or lives; at that time, I and the assembly of monks together emerged from Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.
It is further said: "My pure land is not destroyed, yet the multitudes perceive it as being utterly consumed by fire, filled with such pervasive grief, fear, and suffering.
These sinful beings, due to the causes and conditions of their evil karma, shall not hear the names of the Triple Gem for incalculable eons."
...and so forth, as extensively explained.

Do not harbor the thought that this land is impure, for this buddha-field is supremely pure.

The sixth heaven of the desire realm is named Paranirmita-vaśavartin; because others manifest various objects of sensual desire and one attains great mastery over them to enjoy them, this is the most supreme [heaven] and is thus employed as a metaphor.

This demonstrates that when the mind of a bodhisattva is pure, they perceive a pure land.

With an inner mind that is equanimous and adorned with pure merit, and likewise perceiving the Buddha’s intention to be pure, one sees the buddha-field as supremely pure; therefore, the lands seen by bodhisattvas of the tenth stage are always extremely pure.

The older text differs slightly; where it says "those who do not rely on the Buddha’s wisdom," it appears at first glance as if they simply do not cultivate the Buddha’s wisdom.
